title: Testcontainers and realistic backend integration
description: Use Testcontainers to spin up real databases and services in integration tests, catching schema and query bugs that in-memory fakes miss.

data.text: In-memory databases are convenient, but they lie. SQLite behaves differently from PostgreSQL. Prisma's SQLite generator skips features like JSON columns, enums, and certain constraints that your production database supports. Testcontainers solves this by starting a real Docker container — PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis — during your test run, so your tests execute against a database that matches production.

For a senior frontend engineer, Testcontainers is most useful in API integration and end-to-end tests where the frontend talks to a real backend. It is not a replacement for unit tests, but it fills the gap between mocked unit tests and full-stack E2E tests.

items: Your schema uses production-only features (JSON columns, PostGIS, enums) that SQLite does not support.
You have experienced bugs from ORM dialect differences between dev and production.
Your team owns the backend API and can run it in a container alongside the database.
You want CI to catch migration failures before they reach production.

data.title: Performance and CI considerations
data.text: Starting Docker containers is slower than in-memory tests. Use Testcontainers for a focused integration suite, not for hundreds of unit-style tests. In CI, reuse the Docker layer cache and run container tests in a dedicated job so they do not block faster unit test runs.

items.title: In-memory database
items.description: Fast, but dialect differences hide bugs. Good for unit-style logic tests.

items.title: Testcontainers
items.description: Slower, but production-accurate. Good for migration, schema, and query integration tests.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: Testcontainers starts real services in Docker during tests, eliminating dialect and schema mismatches.
Use it for integration tests that verify Prisma queries, migrations, and API routes against PostgreSQL.
Combine it with a smaller in-memory suite for fast feedback loops.
Keep container tests in a separate CI job to protect overall pipeline speed.
